[USER] User expresses a belief that parody often relies on satire to make its point.  
[USER] User questions how the satirical nature of parody contributes to its artistic merit.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant states that it is generally accepted that parody often relies on satire to make its point.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant explains that satire uses humor, irony, ridicule, or exaggeration to criticize or expose flaws, vices, or absurdities.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant defines parody as a form of art or entertainment that imitates or mocks the style, format, or content of an existing work for comedic effect.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant notes that satirical parody can expose flaws and absurdities of the original work and comment on broader social or cultural issues.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant mentions that satirical parody can be effective because it uses humor to draw attention to serious issues, making them more accessible and engaging.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant states that parody can have artistic merit due to the skill and creativity required to create it.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant acknowledges that there are limits to the use of satire in parody and that it can cross a line to become offensive or disrespectful.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant explains that parodies mocking individuals or groups based on identity aspects may be considered offensive.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant mentions that parodying works dealing with tragedy, suffering, or illness can be inappropriate.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Assistant emphasizes that while parody is a form of free speech, it is not immune to criticism or consequences.
